prompt: According to special relativity, how fast does light travel toward an observer who is running toward the light source?
options: Faster than c — relative velocities add
Slower than c — the observer's motion subtracts
Exactly c — the speed of light is the same in all inertial frames
Depends on the frequency of the light
correctAnswer: Exactly c — the speed of light is the same in all inertial frames
explanation: This is Einstein's second postulate. Unlike sound or bullets, light always travels at c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s in all inertial frames, regardless of the motion of source or observer. This counterintuitive fact was confirmed by the Michelson-Morley experiment (1887) and is the root cause of time dilation, length contraction, and all relativistic effects.

prompt: At v = 0.6c, the Lorentz factor γ = 1/√(1 − v²/c²) = ?
explanation: γ = 1/√(1 − 0.6²) = 1/√(1 − 0.36) = 1/√0.64 = 1/0.8 = 1.25. This means a clock moving at 0.6c runs at 1/1.25 = 80% the rate of a stationary clock. A ruler is 80% of its rest length. To reach γ = 2 you need v = 0.866c; for γ = 10, v = 0.995c.

prompt: Muons created in the upper atmosphere (at ~15 km altitude) travel at 0.998c and have a half-life of ~2.2 μs. Classically they should travel ~660 m before decaying. Why do large numbers reach sea level?
options: Muons are given extra energy by the atmosphere
Time dilation — moving muons' clocks run slow, extending their apparent lifetime in Earth's frame
Length contraction makes the atmosphere thinner
Muons are protected by Earth's magnetic field
correctAnswer: Time dilation — moving muons' clocks run slow, extending their apparent lifetime in Earth's frame
explanation: At v = 0.998c, γ ≈ 15. In Earth's frame, muon lifetime is dilated: 15 × 2.2 μs ≈ 33 μs. Distance covered: 0.998c × 33 μs ≈ 9.9 km — enough to reach sea level. From the muon's frame, the same is explained by length contraction: the atmosphere is 15× thinner (15 km / 15 = 1 km), easily traversed in one half-life. Both frames agree on the outcome.

prompt: Match each relativistic effect to its formula:

pairs.right: Δt′ = γΔt — moving clocks run slow
L = L₀/γ — moving objects are shorter

explanation: All three are consequences of the two postulates of SR. The Lorentz factor γ ≥ 1 quantifies how much time dilates and length contracts. At everyday speeds v ≪ c, γ ≈ 1 and relativistic effects are negligible. At v = 0.99c, γ ≈ 7. At v = 0.9999c, γ ≈ 71.

prompt: The 'twin paradox': one twin travels at 0.8c for 10 years (ship time) and returns. The Lorentz factor at 0.8c is γ = 5/3. How many years have passed on Earth?
correctAnswer: 16.67 years
explanation: The travelling twin ages 10 years (ship time). Earth time = γ × ship time = (5/3) × 10 = 16.67 years. The paradox: why doesn't symmetry apply (each sees the other's clock slow)? Because the travelling twin undergoes acceleration to turn around — breaking the symmetry. The twin who accelerates is younger when they reunite. Confirmed by Hafele-Keating experiment (1971) flying atomic clocks around the world.

prompt: E = mc² tells us that mass and energy are:
options: Different forms of the same thing — interconvertible
correctAnswer: Different forms of the same thing — interconvertible
explanation: Mass-energy equivalence: mass is a form of energy (rest energy). E₀ = mc². In nuclear reactions, a small fraction of mass is converted to kinetic energy (and radiation) — explaining the enormous energy release. The Sun converts ~4 million tonnes of hydrogen mass to energy per second. The mass deficit in nuclear binding (binding energy) also follows from E = mc².

prompt: What is the rest energy (in joules) of a 1 kg mass? (c = 3 × 10^8 m/s). Express as a number × 10^16.
explanation: E = mc² = 1 × (3×10⁸)² = 9×10¹⁶ J. This is about 21 megatons of TNT equivalent. Even a paperclip (1 g) contains 9×10¹³ J. The reason we don't access this energy easily is that converting mass to energy requires nuclear reactions or matter-antimatter annihilation — not available with ordinary chemistry.

prompt: Why can no massive object be accelerated to exactly the speed of light?
options: There is an absolute speed limit enforced by a physical barrier
Relativistic momentum p = γmv diverges as v → c, requiring infinite energy
The object would travel back in time
correctAnswer: Relativistic momentum p = γmv diverges as v → c, requiring infinite energy
explanation: As v → c, γ → ∞, so p = γmv → ∞. Kinetic energy KE = (γ−1)mc² also → ∞. You'd need infinite energy to reach c. Massless particles (photons, gravitons) travel at c always — they have no rest frame. Massive particles always travel at less than c in any inertial frame.

prompt: Using E² = (pc)² + (mc²)², what is the energy of a photon with momentum p = 2 × 10⁻²⁷ kg·m/s? (c = 3 × 10⁸)
explanation: For a photon, m = 0: E = pc = 2×10⁻²⁷ × 3×10⁸ = 6×10⁻¹⁹ J. This corresponds to frequency f = E/h = 6×10⁻¹⁹ / 6.63×10⁻³⁴ ≈ 9×10¹⁴ Hz — ultraviolet light. The relation E = pc for massless particles follows from the general formula E² = (pc)² + (mc²)² when m = 0.

prompt: Match each concept to its spacetime significance:

pairs.right: Events can be causally connected — one can influence the other
Events cannot be causally connected — no signal can reach between them
Events connected by a light signal — on the light cone

explanation: The spacetime interval ds² = −(cdt)² + dx² + dy² + dz² is invariant — all observers agree on it. Its sign determines the causal structure of spacetime. Only timelike-separated events can have a cause-effect relationship. Spacelike-separated events can appear in either order in different frames — there's no invariant 'before' or 'after' between them.

prompt: The equivalence principle states that:
options: Gravitational and inertial mass are the same — gravity and acceleration are locally indistinguishable
The speed of light is the same in all frames
correctAnswer: Gravitational and inertial mass are the same — gravity and acceleration are locally indistinguishable
explanation: Standing in a gravitational field of g and being accelerated at g in deep space are physically identical locally — no experiment inside a sealed box can distinguish them. This led Einstein to the conclusion that gravity is not a force but a curvature of spacetime: free fall is actually the 'straight-line' (geodesic) motion through curved spacetime.

prompt: GPS satellites must correct their atomic clocks by approximately how many microseconds per day due to combined relativistic effects? (GR speeds them up ~45 μs/day; SR slows them ~7 μs/day)
explanation: Net correction = GR effect − SR effect = 45 − 7 = 38 μs/day. GPS clocks are preset to run slightly slower before launch to compensate. Without this correction, GPS positions would drift by ~10 km per day. The fact that GPS requires GR corrections is perhaps the most commercially important test of Einstein's theory.

prompt: Eddington's 1919 eclipse expedition confirmed general relativity by measuring:
options: The bending of starlight passing near the Sun
correctAnswer: The bending of starlight passing near the Sun
explanation: During a total solar eclipse, Eddington photographed stars near the Sun's edge. Their apparent positions shifted by 1.75 arcseconds — twice what Newtonian gravity predicts, exactly matching GR. This made headlines worldwide: 'Lights All Askew in the Heavens — Einstein's Theory Triumphs'. It was GR's first major observational confirmation beyond the Solar System context.

prompt: In the Einstein field equations G_μν = (8πG/c⁴)T_μν, what do the tensors represent?
options: G_μν is mass, T_μν is energy
G_μν describes spacetime curvature; T_μν describes matter and energy content
G_μν is Newton's constant; T_μν is temperature
correctAnswer: G_μν describes spacetime curvature; T_μν describes matter and energy content
explanation: The Einstein tensor G_μν encodes the curvature of spacetime (derived from the Riemann curvature tensor). The stress-energy tensor T_μν encodes all forms of energy and momentum: mass, kinetic energy, pressure, stress. The equation reads: curvature = 8πG/c⁴ × energy content. Mass-energy curves spacetime; curved spacetime guides mass-energy. Two sides of one unified description.

prompt: Match each GR prediction to the experiment that confirmed it:

pairs.right: Eddington eclipse expedition (1919)
Pound-Rebka experiment (1959)
GPS satellite clock corrections

explanation: Each GR prediction has been confirmed to high precision. The 1919 eclipse confirmation made Einstein world-famous overnight. Pound-Rebka measured redshift over just 22.5 m (tiny Δf/f ~ 10⁻¹⁵) using the Mössbauer effect. GPS is the daily operational confirmation — it would fail without GR corrections. GR is now one of the best-tested theories in science.

prompt: What is the Schwarzschild radius?
options: The radius at which a star becomes a neutron star
The radius at which escape velocity equals the speed of light — the event horizon
The orbital radius of the innermost stable orbit
correctAnswer: The radius at which escape velocity equals the speed of light — the event horizon
explanation: r_s = 2GM/c². For any mass, if compressed inside this radius, it becomes a black hole with an event horizon at r_s. For Earth (6×10²⁴ kg), r_s ≈ 9 mm. For the Sun (2×10³⁰ kg), r_s ≈ 3 km. For a 10⁹ solar mass galaxy-centre black hole, r_s ~ 3 × 10¹² m (about 20 AU).

prompt: Calculate the Schwarzschild radius of the Sun in km. (G = 6.67×10⁻¹¹, M_Sun = 2×10³⁰ kg, c = 3×10⁸ m/s). Round to nearest whole km.
explanation: r_s = 2GM/c² = 2 × 6.67×10⁻¹¹ × 2×10³⁰ / (3×10⁸)² = 2.67×10²⁰ / 9×10¹⁶ ≈ 2967 m ≈ 3 km. The Sun is about 700,000 km in radius — 200,000× larger than its Schwarzschild radius. To become a black hole, you'd have to compress the entire Sun into a sphere 3 km across.

prompt: From an outside observer's perspective, what happens to a clock as it falls toward a black hole's event horizon?
options: It speeds up as it falls into stronger gravity
It appears to slow down, approaching a standstill at the horizon, never quite crossing
It crosses the horizon quickly and disappears
It reverses direction due to tidal forces
correctAnswer: It appears to slow down, approaching a standstill at the horizon, never quite crossing
explanation: Gravitational time dilation slows the infalling clock infinitely near r = r_s. From outside, the clock slows, redshifts, and asymptotically approaches the horizon — the outside observer never sees it cross. From the infaller's own perspective, they cross the horizon in finite proper time and nothing special happens locally (for a large enough black hole). Both perspectives are valid in their own frames.

prompt: The Event Horizon Telescope (2019) imaged M87*, a black hole 6.5 billion solar masses. It showed a bright ring with a dark central shadow. What creates the shadow?
options: A cloud of dark matter around the black hole
The event horizon absorbs all light — no photons from inside can escape
The accretion disk blocks the view
correctAnswer: The event horizon absorbs all light — no photons from inside can escape
explanation: The dark shadow (actually 2.6× the event horizon diameter due to gravitational lensing) is a region from which no light escapes — defining an event horizon. The bright ring is hot plasma in the accretion disk, whose light is bent by extreme gravity into a photon ring. The shape and size perfectly match GR predictions for a 6.5-billion-solar-mass Kerr black hole. Sgr A* was imaged similarly in 2022.

prompt: Match each black hole observation to its significance:

pairs.right: Proves 4 million solar mass compact object — Nobel 2020 (Genzel, Ghez)
First direct gravitational wave detection — binary black hole merger
First direct visual evidence of an event horizon shadow

explanation: Black holes went from theoretical curiosity to observationally confirmed objects in just a few decades. Each observation was a Nobel Prize-level result. Together they confirm GR in the strong-field regime and establish black holes as real astrophysical objects — not just mathematical solutions to Einstein's equations.

prompt: Gravitational waves from GW150914 were so small that LIGO's 4 km arms changed length by approximately:
options: A thousandth the diameter of a proton (10⁻¹⁸ m)
correctAnswer: A thousandth the diameter of a proton (10⁻¹⁸ m)
explanation: The strain was h ~ 10⁻²¹. Length change = h × arm length = 10⁻²¹ × 4×10³ = 4×10⁻¹⁸ m ≈ 1/1000 of a proton diameter (~10⁻¹⁵ m). This is the most sensitive length measurement ever made, achieved by laser interferometry with 4 km arms and quantum noise reduction. Two black holes each ~30 times the Sun's mass merged, releasing more power than all stars in the observable universe combined — briefly.

prompt: Hubble's law v = H₀d describes the expanding universe. What does it imply about distant galaxies?
options: They are moving through space away from us
The space between us and them is expanding — they recede faster if they are farther away
They are older and therefore slower
They are moving toward a common centre
correctAnswer: The space between us and them is expanding — they recede faster if they are farther away
explanation: The expansion is not a motion through space — it's an expansion of space itself. Every patch of space grows, so galaxies farther away recede faster (more space between us expanding). The Big Bang was not an explosion from a point — it was the rapid expansion of all of space simultaneously. There is no centre. Every observer sees all other galaxies receding.

prompt: The Penrose-Hawking singularity theorems, and Roger Penrose's Nobel Prize (2020), were for proving that ______ are an inevitable consequence of GR under general conditions.
correctAnswer: singularities
explanation: Penrose (1965) proved that once a trapped surface forms (inside a collapsing star), a singularity is inevitable — no special symmetry or pressure can prevent it. Hawking extended this to cosmological singularities (Big Bang). These theorems showed GR predicts its own failure, making quantum gravity not just interesting but mandatory. Penrose shared the 2020 Nobel with Genzel and Ghez.

prompt: The cosmological constant Λ, originally introduced by Einstein to create a static universe, is now interpreted as:
options: Dark energy driving the accelerating expansion of the universe
correctAnswer: Dark energy driving the accelerating expansion of the universe
explanation: Einstein introduced Λ in 1917 to balance gravity in a static universe (then the prevailing view). When Hubble discovered expansion in 1929, Einstein dropped Λ, calling it his 'greatest blunder'. In 1998, Perlmutter, Schmidt, and Riess (Nobel 2011) discovered the expansion is accelerating — requiring exactly a cosmological constant (or dark energy). Λ turns out to be the dominant energy component of the universe (~68%).

prompt: Match each gravitational wave source to the observation:

pairs.right: GW150914 — first direct GW detection (LIGO 2015)
GW170817 — first multi-messenger GW + electromagnetic observation
Indirect GW evidence from orbital energy loss — Nobel 1993

explanation: Gravitational wave astronomy is less than a decade old but already transformative. GW150914 confirmed binary black holes exist. GW170817 (with simultaneous gamma ray burst, optical afterglow, etc.) confirmed neutron star mergers create heavy elements (gold, platinum) via r-process nucleosynthesis. The Hulse-Taylor pulsar inspired theorists for 40 years before direct detection was possible.

prompt: Why can no massive object reach the speed of light?
options: Its kinetic energy γmc² becomes infinite as v → c
correctAnswer: Its kinetic energy γmc² becomes infinite as v → c
explanation: γ = 1/√(1−v²/c²) diverges. Pushing a particle closer to c requires increasingly more energy per Δv. No finite source can supply infinite energy.

prompt: The energy-momentum relation E² = (pc)² + (mc²)² implies for a photon (m = 0):
correctAnswer: E = pc
explanation: Set m = 0: E² = (pc)², so E = pc. Photons have momentum p = E/c despite being massless. This is the basis of radiation pressure and photon cooling.

prompt: An LHC proton has γ ≈ 7000. From the proton's perspective, the LHC ring (27 km in lab frame) appears:
options: About 1 m around (Lorentz contracted by γ)
correctAnswer: About 1 m around (Lorentz contracted by γ)
explanation: 27 km / 7000 ≈ 3.9 m circumference in the proton's instantaneous rest frame. Lab time of one orbit (~89 μs) shrinks by γ to about 12 ns of proton-frame time. Relativity at extreme.

prompt: Cosmological redshift z is interpreted as a Doppler shift due to galactic recession.
correctAnswer: True
explanation: Roughly true for nearby objects. More accurately, redshift on cosmological scales is from the expansion of space itself — the same wavelength stretching as the universe expands. Both pictures give matching predictions for low z.

prompt: Match the limit to the relativistic relation:

pairs.right: E = mc²
E = pc
E² = (pc)² + (mc²)²

explanation: These three relations are limits of the same equation. They unify mass, energy, and momentum into one Lorentz-covariant 4-vector.

prompt: The Eddington 1919 eclipse expedition tested:
options: Light deflection by the Sun's gravity (gravitational lensing)
correctAnswer: Light deflection by the Sun's gravity (gravitational lensing)
explanation: Stars apparently shifted near the eclipsed Sun by amounts predicted by GR but twice the Newtonian gravity prediction. This made Einstein famous worldwide.

prompt: An Einstein ring forms when:
options: A massive object lies exactly on the line of sight to a distant source, creating a ring of lensed light
correctAnswer: A massive object lies exactly on the line of sight to a distant source, creating a ring of lensed light
explanation: Perfect alignment + axially symmetric lens → ring image. Imperfect alignments give arcs or multiple images. Beautiful and informative.

prompt: The Bullet Cluster shows lensing mass offset from X-ray-emitting hot gas. This is strong evidence that:
options: Dark matter is real and dominates over visible matter
Gravity is repulsive at galactic scales
correctAnswer: Dark matter is real and dominates over visible matter
explanation: In the cluster collision, the dissipationless dark matter passed through, while collisional gas slowed. Lensing tracks the bulk of the mass — and it sits with the dark matter, not the gas. Modified gravity theories struggle to explain this offset.

prompt: Microlensing has been used to detect exoplanets.
correctAnswer: True
explanation: When an exoplanet passes near the line of sight to a background star, it adds a brief, characteristic perturbation to the lensing light curve. Microlensing favors planets at large orbital radii, complementing transit and radial-velocity methods.

prompt: Match the lensing regime to its scientific use:

pairs.right: Multiple images and arcs from massive clusters
Statistical shape distortions — maps dark matter
Brief brightening — finds exoplanets and dim stars

explanation: Lensing regimes are categorized by image multiplicity and observable signatures. Each gives a different window on mass distributions across cosmic scales.

prompt: GPS clocks tick faster than ground clocks because:
options: GR effect (weaker gravity at altitude) outweighs SR effect (motion-induced slowdown)
correctAnswer: GR effect (weaker gravity at altitude) outweighs SR effect (motion-induced slowdown)
explanation: +45 μs/day from gravity, -7 μs/day from velocity, net +38 μs/day. Without correcting both effects, position errors grow 10 km/day. Engineers actively program the offset into satellite clocks.

prompt: Why do cosmic-ray muons reach the Earth's surface despite their short lifetime (2.2 μs)?
options: Time dilation extends their effective lifetime in our frame; length contraction shortens the atmosphere in theirs
Cosmic rays do not produce muons
correctAnswer: Time dilation extends their effective lifetime in our frame; length contraction shortens the atmosphere in theirs
explanation: Both pictures (lab frame vs muon frame) give the same answer: many muons survive to ground level. This was one of the first direct, unambiguous tests of special relativity.

prompt: Distant supernovae fade more slowly than nearby ones because of:
correctAnswer: Cosmological time dilation by factor (1+z)
explanation: Type Ia supernova light curves are standardized, so the (1+z) stretch is unambiguous. Beautiful confirmation of cosmological time dilation.

prompt: Relativity is detectable only in particle accelerators and astrophysics, never in everyday devices.
correctAnswer: False
explanation: GPS, MRI, semiconductors, and even color of gold (relativistic electron behavior in heavy elements) all rely on relativity at one level or another. Relativity is in your phone.

prompt: Match the relativistic effect to its everyday signature:

pairs.right: Combined SR + GR effects, +38 μs/day
Direct test of time dilation
Cosmological time dilation

explanation: Each is a measurable, routinely observed phenomenon driven by relativity. The theory has gone from revolutionary curiosity to engineering necessity in a century.
